title: Why Your Preschooler Is Hitting, Biting, or Kicking (And What Helps)
dek: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting, and kicking are often the only tools left to shout, "I have no say" — when adults control nearly every aspect of their body. Give back a little choice, and the behavior will decrease.
why: Most approaches repeat "no hitting" and add punishment, without touching the need behind the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal, and demonstrates scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers.
who: Parents whose child just started preschool and who often get complaint calls; and preschool teachers who want to reduce aggressive behavior in class without relying on punishment.
skip: After 16:57 it's a course pitch; if you only want the methods, you can skip it.

points.h: Hitting is a child's cry that their body isn't theirs
points.body: Preschool is often the first place where a child's body is controlled by adults other than parents — where to sit, how to sit, when to speak and move. In the previous three years, he could largely decide when to run and when to go to the bathroom. Sitting on the carpet for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old lacks the language to assert "my body, my say," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools left. So when you get a complaint call, don't rush to scold "keep your hands to yourself"; ask instead: how much say did this child have over his own life before, and what can you give back now?

points.h: Kindergarten readiness is really obedience training
points.body: Teachers often say a preschool has a high proportion of children who are kindergarten-ready, and the core definition of that readiness is compliance: when the teacher says sit, you sit — even if you're mid-task, even if your body is overloaded. Parents worry that if the child doesn't comply now, he won't get into a good elementary school, college, or good life. But the price the child pays for this definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either; they themselves need competence, child safety, ease, and even a sense of power; many entered education to repair their own childhood trauma, yet only know power-over relationships. Seeing both sides' positions creates room for negotiation.

points.h: We accommodate ourselves but refuse to accommodate children
points.body: Adults, when they feel overloaded at a party, will arrive early, leave early, retreat to a quiet room, or even wear noise-canceling earplugs — we find this natural. But when it comes to children, aside from routine things like extended test time, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, and he won't survive in the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more accommodation than they allow children. The original provides a concrete image: a bigger, stronger adult picks you up without explanation and carries you from a quiet room back to the middle of a noisy party — if it happened to an adult, you'd immediately see it as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child, we turn a blind eye.

points.h: The fix is before the behavior, not in the behavior itself
points.body: Repeating "no biting" doesn't work because that's not the knowledge the child lacks. You need a different set of questions: what happened in the seconds before the bite? What else happened earlier that day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life? A sensory-overloaded child who loses control when pushed in line — let him stand at the front, back, or outside the line; a child who struggles with transitions needs a few minutes' warning. Analogy to adults: when your partner snaps at you in the evening over nothing, it's often not about the current remark but the morning argument, lack of sleep, and a string of stressors. If the other person then says "your attitude needs adjusting," you'd explode too; yet we often only do the latter to children.

points.h: Talking to the teacher: don't blame, listen to the 'no'
points.body: Telling the teacher "please change your approach" will almost certainly hit a wall. A safer opening is to set aside judgment and reconstruct the facts: not who's responsible, just what actually happened; and include family changes, which are context the teacher can't see. After identifying whether the trigger is sensory or autonomy, then empathize with the three things behind the teacher's behavior: competence, child safety, and a breather of ease. The request must land on a concrete, executable change, like "Can the child sit on a ball outside the circle?" If the teacher refuses, the key isn't the refusal but what need the "no" is still protecting — find a way that meets both sides.

Jen's daughter Carys, at age three, couldn't nap; the teacher required her to lie down, and she was bored and frustrated — her need was to play; the teacher had two needs: state regulations required offering nap time, and nap time was also the teacher's break. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separated corner, where she could quietly play with soft toys that didn't roll, while the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and the break, and Jen escaped the dilemma of complaint calls. This segment shows that "negotiating by needs" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need is preserved.

points.h: All methods boil down to one question
points.body: Compress all the above into one sentence: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop," and ask instead "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting, and kicking are surface signals; the real message might be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my body." Once the need is correctly named, a path to meet it can be designed; and it's almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how adults show up is easier than changing the child.

terms.def: The basic need to have choice over one's life and body and to act according to one's own will.
A preschool metric for whether a child can sit still, follow instructions, and adapt to group rules.
A change to the environment, rules, or arrangements to match an individual's sensory or other needs.
An interaction pattern where the adult is in a superior position and treats the child with commands and domination, as opposed to a collaborative model.

quotes.text: hitting or kicking can be one of the only tools that a three or four-year-old has for saying I don't have any say over what happens to my body right now and I need some of that.
When we imagine it happening to an adult we can kind of see it's an obvious violation of that person's body autonomy. And it is for a child too, it's just that we don't see it that way.
Being kindergarten ready means the child has learned that they are to do what an adult says even if that goes against what they know is right for their body.

But when we think about accommodations for kids unless it's for something like more time when they're taking a test we worry that they won't be able to survive in the real world if we accommodate them too much.
We know that we want that for ourselves, but somehow when kids are involved, we only focus on the behavior that we don't want to see and how do we change that?
And if the teacher says no, which they may do, what you're really listening for is what need they're trying to meet that underlies that no.
What need is this behavior communicating? Because from there you can find strategies to meet everyone's needs.
